Unilever (ULVR-GB) · Triaging A&J Memo · 23-Nov-26

Unilever: a quality staple whose cause for concern is clearing, worth about +14% over 18 months, but without the earnings step-up that drives upgrades

~6%earnings per share growth a year, in line with consensus
+14%probability-weighted return over 18 months
16.05xtwo-year forward P/E, at the 28th percentile of ten years
25%of brokers rate the shares a buy
11-Feb-27full-year results answer two of the three tests

The decision in four points

  1. Unilever's investment case is dependable but not unusually skewed. Earnings per share growth of about 6%, a 3.3% dividend yield and a small re-rating give a probability-weighted return of about +14% over 18 months (roughly 9% a year), with about (6)% in the worse case.
  2. The upside comes from the multiple and the dividend, not from upgrades. Guidance is more likely to be met than raised, and consensus earnings have about plus or minus 2% of room either way.
  3. The single piece of evidence that would create an unusual positive skew is volume of 2% or more while prices rise. The full-year results on 11-Feb-27 will show whether price and volume can rise together.
  4. The Financial Analyst's model of record is more cautious than this memo. The model puts FY2026 earnings per share at €3.04 against my €3.22, and its return at the guideline multiple is +22.3%, not +33%, because the model starts from a two-year forward multiple of 17.6x, not 16.05x (topics #6 and #12).

#0The investment case

1

The one idea: Unilever's everyday brands win where distribution decides the sale. Unilever sells low-priced daily brands (Dove, Vaseline, Rexona and laundry products) through a distribution network that rivals find hardest to copy in emerging markets, which will supply 62% of turnover once Foods leaves. The company keeps a gross margin near 47% and spends about 16% of sales on brand support to hold its volume. Three consequences follow from that business model:

  • Unilever's competitive position is strongest where distribution decides the sale (India, Brazil) and weakest where the retailer decides it (Europe, the US club channel).
  • Unilever's main risk is that raising prices to cover oil- and palm-linked costs loses the volume it has just rebuilt.
  • Unilever's euro earnings swing with currencies, because 86% of revenue is earned outside the euro area.
62%of remaining turnover from emerging markets
~47%gross margin
~16%of sales spent on brand support
86%of revenue earned outside the euro area
2

The change: three real forces support steady growth.

Volume-led growthVolume has grown about 3% a year for 11 quarters, 2026 guidance was raised twice, and the household and personal care business grew 6.9% in the third quarter of 2026.
A simpler companyIce Cream was demerged in December 2025, and Foods is due to combine with McCormick by mid-2027 for US$15.7bn of cash plus McCormick shares, leaving a pure household and personal care business.
Cost and accountabilityA new €1bn savings programme runs to 2029, and profit responsibility returns to six regions from 1-Jan-27.

Together the three forces support underlying sales growth of 4% to 6% and the margin gains that management itself calls "modest". The result is steady compounding, not a step-up in earnings power.

The headwinds are equally real: input-cost inflation of €550m to €1bn in 2027, falling volume in developed markets, a shrinking Wellbeing business, and €400m to €500m of overheads that will be stranded when Foods leaves.

3

How the change reaches the financials: about 6% a year, with no step-up.

  • Sales: underlying sales grow about 4.5% a year.
  • Margin: margin rises only 10 to 20 basis points a year, because stranded costs absorb about half of the €1bn of savings and most of the rest is reinvested in brands.
  • Buybacks: buybacks of €1.5bn a year shrink the share count by about 1.1% a year.

I therefore forecast earnings per share of €3.22 for FY2026, €3.43 for FY2027 and €3.62 for FY2028, growth of about 6% a year. My forecasts sit at the consensus mean for FY2026 and FY2027 and slightly below consensus after that. The Financial Analyst's model of record, calculated after this memo from my inputs, is lower still: €3.04 for FY2026 and €3.30 for FY2027 (topic #6).

So guidance is more likely to be met than raised, and sell-side forecasts have little room to rise.

The larger change is in the narrative. On completion of the Foods deal Unilever becomes a pure household and personal care company, yet only 25% of brokers rate the shares a buy, and the two-year forward multiple of 16.05x sits at the 28th percentile of its ten-year range.

4

The foundation: proven brands and distribution, a short record on euro earnings, and a new team.

Proven

25 power brands produce about 80% of turnover, return on invested capital is 19%, and cash conversion was about 100% in 2025. Since 2024 the company has delivered well on volume and on its guidance.

Not yet proven

Unilever has turned little of that delivery into euro earnings: underlying earnings per share rose 0.7% in 2025, and consensus for FY2027 is 5% lower than a year ago despite the beats. Management is energetic but new: the chief executive has 21 months in the role, 90% of the top team was replaced in three years, and the operating model set in 2022 is being reversed in 2027.
5

The setup: a cause for concern clearing in a quality staple. The best-fitting setup is 'CfC Clearing in HQ low-cyclicality business on Q1/Q2 multiple, leading to reversion to normal': a cause for concern clearing in a high-quality, low-cyclicality business whose multiple sits in the first or second quartile of its range, leading the multiple back to normal.

The cause for concern arrived in March 2026, when the Foods deal and an input-cost shock took the two-year forward multiple from 18.1x to 14.1x in a month. The multiple is now back at 16.05x.

Present in Unilever's case

A good, low-cyclicality business; a multiple in the second quartile of its range; and dated clearing events (results on 11-Feb-27, completion of the Foods deal by mid-2027).

Missing from Unilever's case

A low entry point, because the multiple has already recovered to 16.05x and the shares are 16% above the spring's month-end lows; a single clean concern, because there are three (the deal, volume under higher prices, and costs); and agreement on what a "normal" multiple is.

The alternative setup, 'Big Corporate Change-driven EPSU' (upgrades to earnings per share driven by large corporate change), describes Unilever's change but not its earnings, because the earnings show no step-up.

6

The reward and the skew: positive, but of ordinary size. Over 18 months I estimate a total return of about +16% if the case plays out as forecast, about +29% if growth and the multiple both do better, and about (6)% if volume slips and the multiple returns to its 2026 low. Weighted by probability, the return is about +14%. At the guideline fair multiple of 19.04x the same arithmetic gives +33%, but I think the guideline multiple is unlikely to be reached within 18 months (topic #11).

The positive skew comes from the multiple and the dividend, not from upgrades, because the chance of guidance or consensus being raised is roughly balanced by the chance of cuts.

7

What has to be true: three dated tests, two of them answered on 11-Feb-27.

Test 1 · 11-Feb-27

Volume holds at 2% or more while price rises to about 2.5% to 3%. The answer comes at the full-year results on 11-Feb-27 (fourth-quarter volume and the FY2027 guidance) and the first-quarter statement in late April 2027. A pass is group volume at or above 2% and developed-market volume no worse than the third quarter's (1.7)%.

Test 2 · mid-2027

The Foods combination completes by mid-2027 and the savings cover the stranded costs. The answer comes with the regulatory clearances in the first half of 2027 and the half-year results in late July 2027, the first accounts on the new footing. A pass is completion on time, the buyback under way and margin not falling.

Test 3 · 11-Feb-27

Gross margin stops falling. The answer comes on 11-Feb-27. A pass is second-half gross margin near the first half's 46.8%, and a 2027 input-cost range no worse than €550m to €750m.

The judgements that move the value of the shares most (FY2027 base: revenue €54.7bn, earnings per share €3.43, 2,144.5m shares, tax 26%)

Each judgement on the operations moves FY2027 earnings per share by only a few percent, and the risks lean downwards. The multiple matters more than any of them.

  1. Volume under higher prices. If FY2027 volume grows 0.9% (Jefferies' forecast) instead of about 2%, revenue is 1.1 points lower, about €600m. At the group's 20% margin the lost revenue costs €120m of operating profit, €89m after tax, or €0.04 a share (1.2)%. At the 60% incremental contribution the company cites, it costs €360m of operating profit, €267m after tax, or €0.125 a share (3.6)%. The larger effect is on the multiple: Jefferies makes the 2% volume floor its test and argues for a de-rating if volume breaks it, and a return to the 2026 low of about 14x would take 12% off the share price.
  2. Input costs and margin. If 2027 input-cost inflation is €1bn instead of €550m and price recovers half of the extra €450m, operating profit is €225m lower, €167m after tax, or €0.08 a share (2.3)%; if price recovers none of it, earnings fall €0.155 a share (4.5)%. Each 50 basis points of margin is worth €273m of operating profit and €0.094 a share (2.7%).
  3. Stranded costs and the deal. If the €450m of stranded cost is offset a year late, earnings are €0.155 a share lower (4.5% of the group's earnings, nearer 6% of the remaining company's). Jefferies' net stranded cost of €250m for FY2027 is worth €0.086 a share (2.5%). A six-month delay to completion defers about 12m shares of buyback, worth only 0.6% of earnings; the real cost of a delay is to the narrative.
  4. Currency. Each 1% of currency translation moves earnings by about 1%, or €0.034 a share. I assume no translation effect in FY2027 and (1)% a year after. A repeat of 2025's (5.9)% would take about €0.20 a share (6%), a full year's growth.
  5. The multiple. Each turn of the multiple is 6.2% of the share price, about 305p. From 16.05x, a move to the ten-year median of 17.0x adds 5.9%, a move to the guideline 19.04x adds 18.6%, and a fall to the 2026 low of 14.2x takes off 11.5%.

#1Operating environment

The operating environment is a moderate tailwind to sales and a headwind to margin: emerging markets carry the growth, while developed markets and input costs hold it back.

Evidence.

The tailwinds are in emerging markets and in the position of large brands

  • Emerging-market demand: emerging-market sales grew 9.5% in the third quarter, with volume up 6.0%; India grew 15% on reviving rural demand, helped by a sales-tax cut worth about 4% on price.
  • Large brands and channels: brokers report big brands regaining share and artificial-intelligence search favouring them, and Unilever has the highest exposure of its European peers to the growing US channels (Amazon, Costco, Walmart).
  • Costs and currency easing at the margin: oil fell below $100 in early November from about $115, and currency translation turned from (4.9)% in the first half to +0.6% in the third quarter.

The headwinds are in developed markets and in costs

  • Developed-market volume: developed-market sales fell 0.9% in the third quarter, with North American volume down 2.5%.
  • Store brands: store brands hold 24.1% of Western European sales, and Costco's Kirkland electrolyte launch hit Liquid I.V. directly.
  • Input costs: a basket of oil, palm and aluminium runs about 20% above a year ago, surfactant prices are rising steeply, and Hindustan Unilever is only 29% hedged on crude oil.
  • Local rivals: Morgan Stanley expects local competitors in emerging-market Home Care to return as their supply recovers.
  • Rates: bond yields near 5% weigh on the multiples of all staples.

Inference: the environment helps the top line more than the bottom line. Emerging-market volume growth is partly cyclical and partly aided by one-off factors; the chief executive himself says India "is not naturally a 15% growth company". Input costs are shifting the mix of Unilever's growth from volume towards price in exactly the half-year now under way.

Against the market. The market reads Unilever's emerging-market strength as durable. I read it as strong but at a peak growth rate, and I agree with the market that developed markets will not help before 2028.

Counter-case and what would change my view. Oil staying below $100, with a stable rupee and real, would let pricing ease and volume hold, which is better than I assume. Two quarters of group volume below 2% with price above 3% would make me more negative.

The operating environment supports the volume part of step 2 of the investment case (the change), and weakens step 2 on costs, where the headwinds are present.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. Emerging markets (62% of the remaining turnover) are a real, partly structural tailwind (third-quarter sales +9.5%, volume +6%), and large brands are gaining from AI search and the growing US channels; but India is flattered by a sales-tax cut, developed-market volume is falling (North America (2.5)%), store brands hold 24% of Western Europe, and EUR 550m-1bn of 2027 input-cost inflation pushes growth from volume to price. Consensus sales growth at the 32nd percentile fits the net result, a moderate tailwind to sales offset by a headwind to margin: a mild net positive, above Kerry's neutral flat-volume world and just below OEM's modestly positive recovery.

#2Corporate change

Unilever's corporate change is large in scale and moderate in its effect on earnings: the change reaches the narrative faster than the numbers.

Evidence: the internal change is unusually large.

  • Portfolio: Beauty, Wellbeing and Personal Care rise to 67% of pro forma turnover from 51%; since 2022 the number of brands has been cut from 370 to 180 and the number of product lines by 40%.
  • Savings: the earlier €800m savings programme finished early, in the first half of 2026; one-third of the new €1bn programme comes from a leaner centre and two-thirds from process and technology.
  • Investment: capital spending rises to 3.6% of sales, more than half of it on productivity projects with paybacks under four years, which management estimates are worth 20 to 30 basis points of gross margin a year.
  • Capital returns: €4.5bn of buybacks over 2027 to 2029, and leverage down to about 1.8 times EBITDA by the end of 2027.
  • Incentives: restructuring costs now count against the profit measure in executive pay, which attacks the old habit of excluding them.
The problems in the change are equally concrete. Restructuring will cost €500m to €600m of cash in 2027. The return to regional profit centres reverses the 2022 operating model, and Jefferies and former executives warn of friction between regional and brand leaders and of lost experience after 7,500 job cuts. The new North America president, the key hire for the main growth market, only starts in January 2027. Wellbeing (about 20% of US gross profit) is not expected to grow again until the second half of 2027.

Inference: the change makes the business better and simpler, but adds little to earnings in the next two years, because the savings first replace what the separation costs. The sector digest worries that Unilever's window of volume growth closes when its savings programme ends. The new €1bn programme answers that worry only in part, because its savings are slower and more dependent on technology than the last programme's.

€1bnnew savings programme to 2029
€400m-500moverheads stranded when Foods leaves
€550m-1bn2027 input-cost inflation
€500m-600mrestructuring cash in 2027

Against the market. Bulls (Bernstein) see a re-rating of the multiple from simplification; bears (Jefferies) see value leaking through tax and stranded costs. I sit between the two: the simplification is worth having, its uplift to earnings is not yet visible, and the files do not let me judge the tax leakage.

Counter-case and what would change my view. If the first €300m to €400m of savings lands in 2027 without a cost in volume, margin could rise 30 basis points a year, not 10 to 20. Evidence of lost shelf space or delayed launches during the 2027 reorganisation would cut the other way.

Corporate change supports step 2 of the investment case (the change) and limits step 3 (how the change reaches the financials).

Score: 65, set by the Rater. The internal change is large and partly proven: Ice Cream demerged, Foods leaving for US$15.7bn plus McCormick shares to make a pure HPC company, the EUR 800m programme finished early, a new EUR 1bn programme, 11 quarters of volume growth under the new strategy and EUR 4.5bn of buybacks; but about half the savings only replace EUR 400-500m of stranded cost, restructuring costs EUR 500-600m of cash in 2027, the 2022 operating model is being reversed with 90% of the top team new, so margin rises only 10-20bp a year and EPS about 6%. I weigh the scale more than the Analyst's 'moderate in earnings effect' does, but the outputs lag, so it sits just below OEM's working acquisition engine and above Odfjell's single deal.

#3Industry, business model, financial profile and management

Unilever's foundation is robust in emerging markets, adequate elsewhere, and led by a strong but lightly tested team.

Evidence.

  • Industry structure: branded manufacturers take the largest profit pool in the chain (gross margins of 45% to 55%), no customer exceeds 10% of group turnover, and suppliers of flavours and chemicals have lost pricing power to large buyers. Retailers, by contrast, are gaining pricing power: promotions are about a third of UK sales, and retailers use their own shopper data to launch store brands.
  • Competitive advantage: in India, Unilever's laundry share is three times the nearest rival's and its skin care share 4.5 times; 1.3 million outlets order through its own app; and it makes soap intermediates in-house. In developed markets the advantage is thinner: US deodorant share fell from 44% to 40%, and the group is often not first or second in its categories.
  • Financial profile, above average but not best in class: Unilever's EBITDA margin of 23% compares with 24% at L'Oréal, 26% at Haleon and 30% at Reckitt, and the remaining business's operating margin of 19.1% is 3 to 4 points below peers'. Operating cash flow less capital spending was €6.5bn in FY2025, about 115% of reported net income; FactSet's lower "free cash flow" of €2.1bn is struck after dividends. Net debt is about 2 times EBITDA on the company's measure.

Management

Fernando Fernandez, chief executive since March 2025 after 37 years in the group, is described by former colleagues as fast, fact-based and impatient with committees. His targets are stretching for a staple: the growth range was raised to 4% to 6% from 3% to 5%, and shareholder return is to rank in the top third of peers. Pay rests on sales growth, return on capital, relative shareholder return and cash, with no earnings-per-share measure that buybacks could flatter.

Governance signals: mixed

Trian sold shares in November 2026 and holds about 1.3%; a director resigned abruptly in October; no executive has bought shares in the market; and Fundsmith sold out in mid-2026.

The evidence on Mr Fernandez is thinner than it looks, because the Leadership Foundations report on file mostly assesses the former chief executive. The evidence on Mr Fernandez consists of 21 months of results and a few expert views.

Inference: a good business with a real moat in emerging markets and an ordinary one in the West, run by a capable operator whose record in the top job is short. The margin gap to peers is an opportunity only if Unilever can close it without giving up volume, and history says that is hard: Morgan Stanley's sharpest point is that Unilever's margin gains from 2017 came at the expense of market share.

Against the market. The market prices Unilever as a second-tier staple (16x earnings against L'Oréal's 27x). I agree with the ranking, but I think the emerging-market franchise deserves more credit than the Western franchise loses.

Counter-case and what would change my view. If regional accountability lifts execution in the West, Unilever's quality rises a notch. If Indian quick-commerce platforms let small brands bypass Unilever's distribution moat, the core advantage erodes, and that would change my view of the foundation.

The business and its management support step 4 of the investment case (the foundation); management's short record is the open point.

Score: 72, set by the Rater. A real moat where distribution decides the sale (India laundry share three times the next rival, 1.3 million outlets on its own app), non-discretionary low-cyclicality demand, 25 power brands at about 80% of turnover, ROIC 19% on the memo's basis (13.5%, 79th percentile, in figures; ROE 92nd; gross margin 73rd) and about 100% cash conversion; against that the Western moat is ordinary (US deodorant share 44% to 40%, retailers gaining power), margins are 3-4 points below peers and a capable chief executive has only 21 months in the job. More than one ordinary part keeps it below Tenaris's 35% global share with switching barriers, but it is clearly above Tele2's single-country oligopoly given its global franchise and returns.

#4Guidance, expectations and delivery

Unilever's guidance is reliable and conservative on volume, but merely fair on earnings.

Evidence: guidance has been set low and beaten on volume. The 2026 volume guidance began at "at least 2%", moved to "around 3%" in July and to "at least 3%" in October. Second-quarter volume growth of 5.5% compared with a consensus of about 2.4%, and first-half earnings per share of €1.61 beat consensus by 1.3%. Management talks expectations down: its margin guidance is only ever "modest", it issues pre-close notes each quarter, and the chief executive tells investors not to extrapolate India and tells brand managers not to be "too greedy" on price.

Start of 2026"at least 2%"volume guidance
July 2026"around 3%"first raise
October 2026"at least 3%"second raise
Q2 outcome5.5%against consensus of about 2.4%

Unilever's record on earnings is weaker than its record on volume. The beats were in revenue, not profit: first-half margin was exactly in line with consensus, gross margin fell 70 basis points, and Morgan Stanley raised its sales forecasts while trimming its earnings forecasts for currency. The medium-term growth range of 4% to 6% is also less conservative than it was, because management has raised it.

Inference. Near-term volume guidance is conservative; the FY2027 margin guidance and the 4% to 6% growth range are fair, not cautious. The 2026 pattern of starting low and raising twice is less likely to repeat in 2027, because price is doing more of the work and the comparisons are harder. My odds for 2027 guidance are: met 60%, raised 25%, cut 15%.

Against the market. Brokers treat Unilever's guidance record as proof of conservatism. I think that view holds for volume and overstates the case for earnings.

Counter-case and what would change my view. FY2027 guidance on 11-Feb-27 that again sets volume at "at least 2%", while the first quarter runs near 3%, would restore the 2026 pattern of beats and raises.

The guidance record supports step 4 of the investment case (the foundation) on delivery, and weakens the link in step 3 from operations to upgrades.

Score: 66, set by the Rater. Volume guidance was set low and raised twice in 2026 (at least 2%, around 3%, at least 3%), Q2 volume of 5.5% beat about 2.4%, the EUR 800m programme came in early and management actively talks expectations down with quarterly pre-close notes; but the beats are in revenue not profit (H1 margin exactly in line, gross margin (70)bp, EPS +0.7% in 2025, FY2027 consensus 5% lower than a year ago, mostly currency), and the raised 4-6% range is now fair rather than cautious. A good record on what it guides, weak in turning it into euro earnings: below Odfjell's beats and above MITIE's thinly documented upgrade record.

#5Operating and financial leverage

Revenue growth at Unilever leads to roughly proportionate, not outsized, profit growth: there is no hidden gearing in the earnings.

Evidence: the mechanics of leverage exist. Incremental volume carries a 60% to 65% contribution; gross margin feeds brand spending, which feeds volume (management's "bank of gross margin"); the savings programme is large; and buybacks add about 1% a year to earnings per share. Yet outsized profit growth has not appeared.

2025

+60bpmargin
+0.7%earnings per share

First half of 2026

+4.8%sales
+2.4%earnings

Inference: Unilever is spending its leverage, by choice and by circumstance. Management reinvests gross margin in brand support (16.1% of sales, against 13% three years ago), currency takes its share, and pricing power is limited where it would be most profitable: volume has tended to fall below 2% whenever price growth exceeded about 2.5%. The honest algebra is therefore 4% to 6% sales growth, plus a little margin, plus 1% from buybacks, less currency: 6% to 8% earnings growth before currency, and about 6% after.

Against the market. Bernstein expects the loop from gross margin to brand spending to volume to compound into a re-rating; Jefferies expects reinvestment to cap margins. On the numbers I am closer to Jefferies; on the quality of what the reinvestment buys I am closer to Bernstein.

Counter-case and what would change my view. Brand spending is above management's own normal range of 15% to 16% of sales, and the new return discipline claims 10% to 15% better returns on media spending. If brand spending drifts to 15.5% of sales with volume intact, 50 basis points of margin appears. Two halves of margin gains above 20 basis points with volume above 2% would make me raise my forecasts.

The absence of hidden gearing limits step 3 of the investment case (how the change reaches the financials).

Score: 58, set by the Rater. The structure has real gears (60-65% incremental contribution on volume, a 47% gross margin feeding brand support that feeds volume, a EUR 1bn cost-out programme, buybacks adding about 1% a year on 2x leverage), but pricing power is limited (volume tends to drop below 2% when price exceeds about 2.5%) and the gearing is spent on brand support at 16.1% of sales and on stranded costs, so sales growth of 4.5% gives EPS growth of about 6%, about 1.3 times against the Universe median of about 2. Moderate gearing on several elements with none proven strong, in the 50s level beside Carlsberg (57).

#6Forecast financials

Forecast earnings growth is mid-single-digit and well supported, not double-digit. That growth rate fixes the size of step 3 of the investment case and caps the return in step 6.

Earnings per share are on the brokers' underlying basis, on which FY2025 was €3.08. FY2029 consensus rests on three brokers. The consensus means for FY2026 and FY2027 are 3.22 and 3.43, the same as my forecasts.

How I tested the forecasts. Past delivery supports the sales line, which relies on strengths the business has already shown. The margin line is where the thesis would need a strength Unilever has not yet shown (closing the margin gap to peers while absorbing stranded costs), so I give margin only the guided "modest" pace. The range of outcomes over 18 months is narrow on operations (sales growth of 3.5% to 6%, margin within 50 basis points of my forecast) and widened by currency and by the separation of Foods. I have taken a currency drag from FY2028, because currency translation cut reported growth in each of the last four years.

Inference: there is no scope for double-digit growth. Growth of about 6% a year is better than the roughly flat euro earnings per share since 2019 (on FactSet's adjusted basis, across a changing group), so growth is higher than in the past, but only to the level of an ordinary good staple. Peers are forecast to grow faster: L'Oréal about 10% and Haleon 7% to 12%.

What these forecasts cannot show: the Foods exit rebases every headline figure

When Foods leaves, reported revenue falls by about a quarter and headline earnings per share fall by about 21% before stranded costs (Redburn). In exchange, shareholders receive McCormick shares worth roughly €10 a Unilever share, about 17% of the share price (my arithmetic from the announced terms and valuation). Consensus has not rebased its headline figures, so every comparison in this memo is on the old footing.

Counter-case. The case for higher numbers is that the €500m of savings left after stranded costs is about 1.3% of the remaining company's sales, enough for 40 basis points of margin a year if none of it were reinvested. The case for lower numbers is a repeat of 2025's currency translation.

Against the market and what would change my view. My forecasts are at consensus or 1% to 3% below it, because I take a currency drag and a slower margin path. FY2027 guidance for more than modest margin gains would lift my numbers; a devaluation of the rupee or the real would cut them.

The Financial Analyst's model: the forecasts of record (model update 1, calculated after this memo from the Analyst's forecast inputs)

#7Scope for upgrades

The scope for upgrades to Unilever's numbers is small and two-sided; the scope for upgrades to its narrative is moderate. Scope for upgrades is the weakest link in step 3 of the investment case and the reason the skew in step 6 is ordinary.

Evidence, counting only what is not already in guidance or consensus:

For upgrades

  • Input costs at the low end: if oil holds below $100, 2027 input-cost inflation nearer €550m than €1bn is worth 1% to 2% on earnings. Brokers already hold this evidence; Deutsche Bank upgraded the shares partly on it.
  • Currency: spot rates imply roughly neutral translation in 2027 after (2)% to (3)% in 2026. Some broker models still carry a currency drag, so the upside is perhaps +1%.
  • Savings arriving early: the last savings programme finished early. Early savings are not in guidance; they are plausible but unquantified.

Against upgrades

  • Stranded costs: Jefferies' net stranded cost of €250m in FY2027 (2.5% of earnings) is not clearly in every broker's model.
  • Wellbeing: Wellbeing stays negative until the second half of 2027.
  • Rebasing: the rebasing of headline figures at completion will scatter estimates for a quarter or two.

Inference: the net scope for consensus earnings is about plus or minus 2%. I cannot name evidence that the sell-side lacks, which is why my forecasts sit at consensus. My odds for FY2027 consensus earnings over the next 18 months are: upgraded by more than 2%, 30%; held within 2%, 45%; cut by more than 2%, 25%. The breadth of revisions should stay mildly positive into February 2027 and flatten by mid-2027. Guidance has more chance of a small raise than a cut (topic #4), but from a base that already assumes delivery.

The scope is larger in ratings and narrative than in numbers. With a quarter of brokers at buy and a mean rating of hold, the completion of the Foods separation and the start of the buyback give analysts a reason to change their ratings, as Deutsche Bank did on 11-Nov-26.

Against the market. Bernstein forecasts FY2027 earnings per share of €3.51 on faster emerging-market volume. I do not, because price is replacing volume. I agree with consensus on the central case.

What would change my view. First-quarter 2027 volume growth above 3% with price growth near 3% would show that both can rise at once, and upgrades would follow.

Score: 51, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is more likely met than raised (60% met, 25% raised, 15% cut), consensus FY2027 EPS has a balanced plus or minus 2% (30% up, 25% down) against about 4.5% revenue growth, so the sized scope is near nil; the narrative has more room (19-25% buy ratings, pure-play completion, buyback start, Deutsche Bank's upgrade). Slightly above Kerry's stuck narrative and below Spie's raised target with turning organic growth.

#8Current momentum

Unilever's momentum is positive but modest: it is turning up from a low base, mainly because peers are weak.

Evidence. The dashboard's pinned ratings (snapshot of 23-Nov-26) are:

Technical momentum CSell-side earnings momentum BValuation B

  • Guidance: two raises in 2026, the latest on 28-Oct-26.
  • Sell-side: consensus FY2027 earnings are up 1% over one and three months and 2% over six months, but down 5% over twelve months; target prices are up 4% in a month; and the share of buy ratings is up 4 points in three months.
  • Narrative: the narrative has improved since the investor event, with a Deutsche Bank upgrade to buy, but remains split, with target prices from 4,000p (Jefferies) to 5,800p (Bernstein).
  • Price: the share price of 4,887.5p is 5.2% above its 200-day average, up 13.0% over six months and flat over twelve; the 200-day average rose in only 3 of the last 12 months; and relative strength is at the 50th percentile.
  • Peers: only L'Oréal is stronger (B and A on the dashboard's ratings). Reckitt (C, D) cut its growth guidance in October; Haleon (D, F) and Beiersdorf (C, F) have falling estimates.

Inference: momentum is turning up from a low base, not strong. Unilever's earnings momentum is the best in the sector bar one because peers are weak, not because Unilever's upgrades are large. The environment is neutral to helpful: the weekly digest rates Consumer staples and Household products Overweight, but notes that the defensive rotation has started to fade and that the sector's own relative strength reads D.

Counter-case. The six-month rise in the share price came with the whole defensive rotation, which the digest says is fading, so the shares' momentum could fade with it.

Against the market. I agree with the dashboard's letters. I would add that a year of estimate cuts has only recently stopped.

What would change my view. A third guidance raise in February 2027, or the 200-day average rising for several months running, would make momentum strong.

Momentum supports step 5 of the investment case (a cause for concern beginning to clear) more than it supports a story of delivery.

Score: 65, set by the Rater. One measure positive, just short of the top fifth, and relative strength exactly neutral make it mixed, so C. Placed in the upper part of the band because guidance was raised twice (latest 28-Oct-26), buy ratings rose 4 points and targets 4% in a month and the narrative is improving, while revisions are small against growth (+1%/+1%/+2%, about 0.2 times), the price is flat over twelve months with the 200-day average rising in only 3 of 12 months, and peers are weak (Reckitt, Haleon, Beiersdorf), which does not lift it.

#9Risk and simplicity

Risk is low for Unilever's business and moderate for its 2027 transition.

Simplicity

The operating case is simple: three numbers (volume, price and gross margin) reported every quarter. The reporting case will not be simple in 2027. Foods deconsolidates, McCormick shares are distributed, service agreements run for two years, segments change from four to three, and stranded costs and tax leakage appear. For a year the accounts will be hard to compare, and that year is when errors of judgement (mine included) are most likely.

Fragilities

The case requires price increases that do not break volume; a savings programme that outruns stranded costs; a deal that closes on time; and currencies that do not repeat 2025.

How the risks arrive. Most of Unilever's risks are slow and trackable through scanner data, quarterly volumes and commodity prices. Three can arrive suddenly:

A commodity or currency shockDeutsche Bank notes that oil spikes have gone with double-digit falls in forward earnings.
A regulatory delay to the dealOne low-grade source reports a UK Phase 2 review, which I cannot verify.
The Brazilian tax dispute€3.56bn is unprovisioned according to the debt prospectus, about €1.65 a share, with timing unknown.

The precedents show that staples de-rate fast when a story breaks. Unilever lost four turns of multiple in March 2026. The 2018 sale of the spreads business diluted earnings per share by 8% through stranded costs. And over-pricing in 2022 and 2023 cut European volume by more than 5%.

Mitigants. Low cyclicality, 90% local-for-local manufacturing, short interest of 0.1%, and a balance sheet that the Foods cash strengthens.

Where the files disagree. The files give conflicting figures for four items; in each case I have used the filing-backed or company figure.

Against the market. The Risks report rates the full bear case as unlikely and an earnings shortfall against consensus as a medium risk. I agree, and would locate the shortfall risk in the margin, not the sales line.

What would change my view. A confirmed Phase 2 review or an adverse Brazilian ruling would raise the risk grade; a clean completion of the deal would lower it.

The low business risk keeps the downside in step 6 of the investment case shallow. The transition risk qualifies step 7 (what has to be true), because two of its three conditions fall inside 2027, the hardest year to read.

Score: 66, set by the Rater. The operating case is simple and low-cyclicality (volume, price, gross margin reported quarterly), the memo's 18-month forward EPS range is EUR 3.65-4.03 around 3.92 (about (7)% to +3%) and leverage is moderate at 2x; but 2027 is a hard year to read (deconsolidation, segment change, stranded cost, tax leakage), currency can take a full year's growth, and three risks can be sudden (an oil or currency shock, a regulatory delay to the deal, an unprovisioned EUR 3.56bn Brazilian tax claim), with a precedent of four turns of de-rating in a month. Wider and more complex than MITIE's offer-anchored case, a little better than OEM's.

#10Lifecycle phase

Unilever's shares are turning up, but are not yet reinforcing in the market's eyes.

Evidence: the operations fit the dashboard's 'Reinforcing' phase; the share price and estimates do not. The dashboard's rule places the stock in Reinforcing, and the operations fit that label: 11 quarters of volume growth and rising guidance. The share price and estimates do not fit it. The shares are flat over twelve months and 12% below their 52-week high, estimates were cut for most of the year, and only a quarter of brokers rate the shares a buy.

Inference. I place the stock between 'turning up' and 'thesis broadening'. The operating thesis is reinforcing, but the market's belief in the thesis was reset in March 2026 and is only now rebuilding. The next change of phase depends on the three tests in topic #0. Passing the tests through mid-2027 moves the stock into broadening, as the pure-play story gains holders. Failing the volume test moves the stock to stalling, which is what Jefferies expects.

Against the market and what would change my view. My placement differs from the dashboard's label by about one phase, and that difference matters for the fair multiple in topic #11. Volume growth above 2% under higher pricing in February 2027 would bring me to the dashboard's reading.

The lifecycle phase supports step 5 of the investment case (the setup) and argues for a lower fair multiple than the guideline's.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo's 'between turning up and broadening' over the computed Stalling, but not with the step towards Broadening: the cause for concern is clearing (guidance raised twice, estimate cuts stopped, buy ratings and targets rising, price 5% above its 200-day) yet growth and margins are steady, not accelerating, upgrades are small and the shares are flat over twelve months. An early turn in the narrative on an unchanged earnings trajectory sits just below Kerry's mid-cycle Reinforcing and above Nexans's paused momentum.

#11The fair multiple

The guideline fair multiple is 19.04x two-year forward earnings, the 90th percentile of the ten-year range, set for a Reinforcing phase. Today's multiple is 16.05x.

My view: 19x is too high as an 18-month outcome on today's footing. About 17x, the ten-year median, is the multiple I would defend, and 16.5x is my base case.

Four reasons the guideline multiple is too high:

  • History: the multiple reached 19x only in 2017 (after the Kraft Heinz approach) and in 2019 and 2020, when bond yields were near zero. In the last five years the multiple ranged from 14.0x to 18.3x, with a median of 16.2x.
  • Rates: bond yields are near 5%, and the weekly digest asks of every case whether its return needs a lower discount rate. At 19x, Unilever's return does.
  • Phase: if the stock is turning up and not reinforcing (topic #10), the guideline itself would point lower in the range.
  • Arithmetic of the separation: Deutsche Bank puts the household and personal care business alone at about 18.8x FY2027 earnings in today's share price, against about 17x for the whole group on the same year. If Deutsche Bank is right, some 1.8 turns of the gap to 19x will close mechanically when the lower-multiple Foods business leaves, without the shareholder gaining anything; the true re-rating on offer is nearer one turn. I cannot reproduce Deutsche Bank's figure from the files, so I hold this point as an inference.

Counter-case. Pure-play household and personal care companies have earned higher multiples, Redburn puts Unilever's shares at a 15% to 20% discount to US peers, and the staples sector as a whole sits near ten-year lows, so a sector re-rating would carry Unilever with it.

What would change my view. Completion of the deal with volume growth above 2% and bond yields falling would make 18x reasonable; all three at once would make 19x arguable.

The guideline multiple is the top of the plausible range, not its centre. That matters directly for step 6 of the investment case: at 19x the multiple supplies more than half of the 18-month return, and I would not count on it.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. Cheap on one measure and dear on the other gives C. Placed low in the band because the own-range cheapness is partly deserved (yields near 5% against a history that includes near-zero rates; the memo itself puts today at the 28th percentile and its fair multiple at only 16.5-17x against 16.05x) and partly an artefact of the perimeter (Deutsche Bank puts the remaining HPC business at about 18.8x already), while the premium to peers is real even if flattered by de-rated peers.

#12Total shareholder return

Probability-weighted: about +14% over 18 months (0.25 × 29.3 + 0.50 × 15.8 - 0.25 × 6.2 = 13.7), roughly 9% a year. Over three years at my 17x, the return is about +35%, or 10.5% a year: earnings +17%, multiple +6%, dividends +11%.

Starting point. The share price was 4,887.5p on 20-Nov-26, about €58.35 at the euro-sterling rate implied by FactSet's two quotes of 16-Nov-26. At 16.05x, that price implies two-year forward earnings of €3.64 a share on consensus.

At the guideline fair multiple of 19.04x, the same arithmetic gives much more, almost all from the multiple:

18 months · about +33%

Forward earnings reach €3.92 on my forecasts (+7.8%); the multiple rises to 19.04x (+18.6%); the share price rises 27.9% (1.078 × 1.186) to about 6,250p; and six quarterly dividends add about €2.90 (+5.0%). The total is about +33%.

Three years · about +50%

Forward earnings reach €4.26 (+17.2%, with FY2031 extrapolated at 5.7% growth); the multiple adds 18.6%; the share price rises 39.0%; and dividends of €6.22 add 10.7%. The total is about +50%, or 14.4% a year.

What drives the return. In my base case about four-fifths of the return is earnings growth and dividends, which are dependable, and one-fifth is the multiple. At the guideline multiple, the multiple supplies more than half of the return. The buyback matters more than its size suggests, because it supplies about 1 point of the 6% earnings growth and depends on the Foods cash arriving. The return is measured in the euro-equivalent share price; a sterling holder also carries the euro-sterling exchange rate.

Against the market. Consensus target prices sit only 4% to 7% above the share price, more cautious than my base case. The gap between the targets and my base case is mostly the dividend and my half-turn of re-rating.

What would change my view. February 2027 results that pass the volume and gross-margin tests would move weight from the worse case to the better case and lift the weighted return towards +17%.

The return is respectable and the downside shallow, but the return is not unusually skewed. That sets step 6 of the investment case: a dependable 9% to 10% a year with an option on re-rating, not an earnings step-up.

#13Summary conclusion

Unilever is a concern clearing in a quality staple: a clear, fairly sure and easily tracked case worth about +14% over 18 months, but without the unusual positive skew in upgrades that Richard prizes most.

Unilever is a good, low-cyclicality business in the middle of a change that is large in form and modest in earnings. The operations are delivering. The shares de-rated in March 2026 on the Foods deal and input costs, and have recovered about half of that de-rating.

The return comes from steady compounding, not upgrades. About 6% earnings growth, a 3.3% dividend yield and perhaps one turn of re-rating give roughly +14% over 18 months on my weighting, with about (6)% in the worse case.

One piece of evidence would add an upgrade story: proof that higher prices and volume growth above 2% can coexist. The case as it stands does not depend on that evidence; the evidence decides whether the case also becomes an upgrade story, and the next two reports (the full-year results on 11-Feb-27 and the first-quarter statement in late April 2027) will show it.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 57, set by the Rater. The input forces are net positive (a mild external tailwind at 55 and a large internal change at 65), but they reach profits weakly because savings fund stranded costs and brand support, so EPS grows about 6%, below the Universe median of 11% (topic 6 C); clearly positive inputs that lift profits only to below-median growth make a mild net positive in the high 50s.
Foundations' Robustness: 76, set by the Rater. Quality at 72 rests on non-discretionary daily brands, a distribution moat in emerging markets, low cyclicality, ROIC of about 19% and full cash conversion, which by Richard's stability test (CVS Group 80) carries it into the 75 band; it stays below 80 because the Western moat and margins are ordinary, the leadership is new and the operating model is being reversed, and delivery (66) is reliable on volume but weak on euro earnings.
Setups' Fit/Crispness: 68, set by the Rater. The case fits 'CfC Clearing in HQ low-cyclicality business' in substance: a good low-cyclicality business, a multiple low in its range and dated clearing events; but the concern is three concerns (the deal, volume under higher prices, input costs) and current problems (falling developed-market volume, gross margin falling, stranded costs, a reorganisation) blur the mechanism. I score higher than the Analyst's C because the recovered entry point is price and timing, which does not count here.
Case Riskiness: 70, set by the Rater. Over topic 9 at 66: a boring, low-cyclicality case whose likely misses are mostly paper cuts (volume a little below 2%, margin flat), with conservative volume guidance and a multiple low in its own range, which Richard's CVS Group example lifts; held below the 75s by the hard-to-read 2027 transition, currency, the unprovisioned Brazilian claim and a precedent of a four-turn de-rating in a month.

How the Financial Analyst's model splits the return. The model's split is on the return's own basis: the two-year forward price-to-earnings multiple and two-year forward earnings per share, today against each horizon. The multiple and earnings parts multiply (1 plus one part, times 1 plus the other, less 1, is the change in the share price); dividends add to that. The template's own split (TSR Dupont sheet, rows 46 and 47) measures the same return on trailing twelve-month earnings and the trailing multiple: at the 18-month column, +1.7% from the multiple and +15.5% from earnings; at the three-year column, +1.0% from the multiple and +26.4% from earnings. That trailing split reads differently when earnings over the next twelve months are flat or falling, so the forward split above is the one to use. The model's two horizons are its fixed columns after the last reported period, so they end on the dates shown, not 18 months and three years from today.
